report.source_text: The patient had a painless rash on the right side of the occipital region (figure 1). Atopic dermatitis was also present on his back and lower legs. He exhibited no nuchal rigidity or jolt accentuation of the neck. Spontaneous back pain consistent with lumbar herniation was noted, but there was no spinal tapping pain. He was oriented to date, location and memory, and no unusual neurological abnormalities were observed.

report.source_text: Meningitis was suspected, and a lumbar puncture was performed immediately. The CSF was clear and colourless, with the following characteristics. Gram staining of centrifuged CSF revealed primarily mononuclear leucocytes, but no bacteria were detected (figure 2). Testing for serum HIV antigen and antibody was negative. Bacterial and mycobacterial cultures were obtained from the CSF, along with two sets of blood cultures. PCR testing for herpes simplex virus (HSV) was performed to assess the need for antiviral therapy. MRI revealed no abnormal intracranial signals.

report.source_text: The patient was then admitted to our hospital. Acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) and ampicillin (2 g every 6 hours) were administered intravenously. Ampicillin treatment was discontinued after blood and CSF cultures tested negative. After hospitalisation, the exudate from a painless skin rash on the right occipital area worsened. A dermatologist evaluated the patient and diagnosed herpes zoster based on the nature, distribution and associated pain of the rash.

report.source_text: The patient’s fever resolved and his symptoms improved. After 5 days of intravenous acyclovir treatment, the patient was discharged with 5 days of oral valacyclovir 1000 mg three times per day.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A young man in his 20s presented with fever, headache, vomiting, back pain, and a painless occipital rash, initially without meningeal signs. CSF analysis revealed mononuclear leukocytes with no bacterial growth and negative HSV PCR. VZV DNA was detected in CSF PCR at high copy number, confirming viral meningitis due to VZV. MRI was normal intracranially. The patient was treated with intravenous acyclovir and briefly with ampicillin, which was discontinued after negative cultures. Dermatologist evaluation of the rash confirmed herpes zoster. The patient’s fever and symptoms resolved after 5 days of IV acyclovir and he was discharged on oral valacyclovir.
